disease.name: Calcium Deficiency
disease.scientific_name: Calcium Deficiency / Hypocalcaemia / Nutritional Calcium Deficiency / Osteoporosis / Osteomalacia / Rickets
disease.icd_10_code: E58 (Dietary calcium deficiency); E55 (Vitamin D deficiency — closely linked); E83.5 (Disorders of calcium metabolism); E55.0 (Rickets, active); M83 (Adult osteomalacia); M80-M81 (Osteoporosis); E20 (Hypoparathyroidism); E83.51 (Hypocalcaemia)

overview.description: Calcium deficiency is a state of inadequate calcium in the body — encompassing a spectrum from nutritional dietary calcium deficiency, acute or chronic hypocalcaemia (low blood calcium), to the long-term skeletal consequences of calcium depletion: osteoporosis, osteomalacia (adults), and rickets (children). Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the human body (approximately 1000-1200g in adults — 99% stored in bones and teeth as hydroxyapatite crystal), and beyond its structural role, calcium is indispensable for: neuromuscular transmission, cardiac electrical conduction, muscle contraction, enzyme function, blood coagulation, and intracellular signalling. Calcium homeostasis is tightly regulated by three hormones — Parathyroid Hormone (PTH), calcitriol (active Vitamin D / 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3), and calcitonin — maintaining serum calcium within the narrow range of 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.12-2.62 mmol/L). Disruption of this regulatory system or prolonged dietary inadequacy leads to a spectrum of manifestations from subtle neurological symptoms (perioral tingling, muscle cramps) to life-threatening tetany, seizures, and cardiac arrhythmias.
overview.affected_organ: Bones and teeth (primary structural store); Neuromuscular system; Cardiac conduction system; Kidneys; Parathyroid-vitamin D axis
overview.prevalence: One of the most common nutritional deficiencies globally. Osteoporosis affects over 200 million people worldwide (1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 will suffer an osteoporotic fracture). Vitamin D deficiency — the most common cause of calcium malabsorption — affects 40-70% of the Indian population. Rickets remains endemic in low-income tropical countries despite adequate sunlight — due to dietary calcium deficiency in low-calcium diets. Hypocalcaemia is found in 15-18% of hospitalised patients.
overview.age_group: All ages; highest clinical impact in: postmenopausal women (osteoporosis), elderly >65 (falls + fractures), children 6 months-5 years (rickets), pregnant/lactating women (increased demand), adolescents (peak bone mass formation).
overview.sex_ratio: Women significantly more affected — particularly postmenopausal women (oestrogen loss dramatically accelerates bone resorption; women have lower peak bone mass than men; longer life expectancy increases fracture risk). Men affected later and less severely but osteoporosis is significantly underdiagnosed in men.
overview.key_fact: Hip fracture from osteoporosis has a 20-30% mortality in the year following the fracture — making osteoporosis-related fractures as serious as many cancers, yet calcium and Vitamin D supplementation with lifestyle measures can reduce fracture risk by up to 40%

calcium_physiology.total_body_calcium: 1000-1200g total body calcium (adults); 99% in bones and teeth (hydroxyapatite — Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2); 1% extracellular (serum and interstitial fluid); <0.01% intracellular (critically important for signalling)

serum_calcium_forms.total_serum_calcium: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.12-2.62 mmol/L) — total measured on routine blood tests
serum_calcium_forms.ionised_free_calcium: ~45% of total; 4.5-5.2 mg/dL (1.12-1.30 mmol/L) — the PHYSIOLOGICALLY ACTIVE form; directly regulates PTH secretion and neuromuscular function
serum_calcium_forms.protein_bound: ~40-45% bound to albumin (major) and globulins; NOT physiologically active

calcium_physiology.albumin_correction: When albumin is LOW (hypoalbuminaemia — common in sick patients, malnutrition, liver disease): CORRECT the measured total calcium. Corrected calcium (mg/dL) = Measured calcium + 0.8 × (4.0 − Serum albumin g/dL). Low albumin gives FALSELY LOW total calcium — corrected calcium may be normal (euCaemia).

hormonal_regulation.PTH: Parathyroid Hormone — secreted by chief cells of parathyroid glands when ionised calcium falls. Actions: RAISES serum calcium by: (1) Osteoclast activation (bone resorption → Ca²⁺ release); (2) Renal calcium reabsorption in DCT; (3) Renal phosphate excretion (phosphaturia); (4) Activation of Vitamin D (1α-hydroxylase stimulation in kidney → calcitriol production)
hormonal_regulation.calcitriol_active_vitamin_D: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 (calcitriol) — the active form. Actions: RAISES serum calcium by: dramatically increasing intestinal calcium absorption (5-10% without Vit D → 30-40% with adequate calcitriol); bone calcium mobilisation; renal calcium reabsorption. Synthesised in skin (UV-B + cholesterol → pre-D3 → D3); 25-hydroxylation in liver → 25(OH)D (storage form, measured in blood); 1α-hydroxylation in kidney → 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol — active)
hormonal_regulation.calcitonin: Secreted by parafollicular C-cells of thyroid when calcium is HIGH. Actions: LOWERS serum calcium by: inhibiting osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; increasing renal calcium excretion. Less physiologically dominant than PTH/calcitriol in humans but used therapeutically (nasal/injectable calcitonin for osteoporosis)

daily_requirements.india_rda: ICMR-NIN RDA India: 600mg/day (lower than Western RDA — Indian diets more typically plant-based calcium with lower bioavailability; Indian guidelines account for this)

types.name: Nutritional Calcium Deficiency (Dietary Inadequacy)
types.description: Chronic inadequate calcium intake without meeting daily requirements — the most common form globally and a major public health issue particularly in low-income countries, vegans, and those avoiding dairy. Long-term dietary calcium inadequacy does not primarily cause low serum calcium (compensated by PTH-mediated bone resorption) but depletes bone mineral density progressively, eventually causing osteoporosis, osteomalacia, or rickets.
types.prevalence: India: typical Indian vegetarian diet provides 300-400mg calcium/day (well below 600mg ICMR recommendation); non-dairy vegetarian diet for vast majority of population relying primarily on grains which are low in bioavailable calcium
types.common_in: Vegans; lactose-intolerant individuals avoiding all dairy; populations with low dairy intake; elderly with poor dietary variety; children with restrictive diets
types.consequences: Osteopenia → Osteoporosis (adults); Rickets (children); Dental caries and enamel hypoplasia; Nutritional calcium-deficiency rickets (endemic Africa, Asia)

types.name: Acute Hypocalcaemia
types.description: Sudden or rapidly developing fall in serum ionised calcium — a medical emergency when severe (<1.1 mmol/L ionised or corrected total calcium <7.5 mg/dL). Causes: post-surgical hypoparathyroidism (most common acute cause — after total thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy); hungry bone syndrome (massive bone uptake post-parathyroidectomy); acute pancreatitis (calcium saponification with fat necrosis); citrate toxicity (massive blood transfusion — citrate chelates calcium); severe hypomagnesaemia; severe sepsis; rhabdomyolysis.
types.clinical_urgency: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — can cause laryngospasm, tetany, cardiac arrhythmias (prolonged QT → torsades de pointes → ventricular fibrillation)
types.treatment: IV calcium gluconate 10% infusion — URGENT; treat underlying cause

types.name: Chronic Hypocalcaemia
types.description: Persistently low serum calcium — most commonly from: hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune, genetic); pseudo-hypoparathyroidism; chronic vitamin D deficiency; chronic kidney disease (reduced calcitriol production + phosphate retention); malabsorption (coeliac, Crohn's, bariatric surgery). Chronic hypocalcaemia may be well-compensated (subtle symptoms) or cause significant neuromuscular, cardiac, and psychiatric symptoms.
types.most_common_causes: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism; autoimmune hypoparathyroidism; chronic Vitamin D deficiency; CKD-mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD)
types.symptoms: Perioral numbness, tingling of hands/feet, muscle cramps, positive Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs, cognitive changes, depression, cataracts (long-term)

types.name: Hypoparathyroidism
types.description: Insufficient PTH production — the most important cause of chronic hypocalcaemia requiring long-term management. Without PTH: intestinal calcium absorption falls; renal calcium wasting increases; bone resorption is suppressed → serum calcium falls. PTH also stimulates Vitamin D activation — deficiency causes functional calcitriol deficiency as well. Characterised by: low calcium, HIGH phosphate (no PTH phosphaturia), and low or inappropriately normal PTH level.
causes: Post-surgical (most common in adults) — after thyroid, parathyroid, or neck surgery
Autoimmune (isolated or as part of APS-1 — autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1)
Genetic (DiGeorge syndrome — 22q11.2 deletion; GCMB mutations; CASR mutations causing activating mutation of calcium-sensing receptor)
Magnesium deficiency (suppresses PTH secretion and PTH action — MUST CORRECT Mg before treating hypocalcaemia)
types.management: Calcium + active Vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol); recombinant PTH (Natpara/PTH 1-84 or teriparatide) in selected refractory cases; avoid hypercalciuria (monitor 24h urinary calcium — risk of renal stones)

types.name: Osteoporosis
types.description: A chronic skeletal disease characterised by reduced bone mass and deterioration of bone microarchitecture — leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. The silent disease — no symptoms until a fragility fracture occurs. WHO definition: Bone Mineral Density (BMD) T-score ≤ −2.5 SD below young adult mean (by DEXA scan). Osteopenia: T-score −1.0 to −2.5. Osteoporosis is the long-term consequence of negative calcium balance, hormonal changes (oestrogen deficiency), genetic factors, and lifestyle over decades.
types.epidemiology: Most common metabolic bone disease globally; 200 million women affected worldwide; 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men >50 will have an osteoporotic fracture; hip fracture is the most devastating complication — 20-30% mortality in the first year

types_within_osteoporosis.primary_type_1: Postmenopausal osteoporosis — oestrogen deficiency accelerates bone resorption; predominantly trabecular bone (vertebral, Colles' fractures); occurs 50-70 years
types_within_osteoporosis.primary_type_2: Age-related (senile) osteoporosis — affects both cortical and trabecular bone; men and women >70 years; hip and long bone fractures predominant
types_within_osteoporosis.secondary: From specific causes: glucocorticoid-induced (most common secondary), hypogonadism, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, IBD, RA, CKD, medications (bisphosphonate overuse causing atypical femoral fractures)

types.who_dexa_criteria: Normal: T-score > -1.0; Osteopenia: T-score -1.0 to -2.5; Osteoporosis: T-score ≤ -2.5; Severe osteoporosis: T-score ≤ -2.5 plus ≥1 fragility fracture

types.name: Osteomalacia (Adults) / Rickets (Children)
types.description: Osteomalacia (adults) and Rickets (children) are diseases of defective bone mineralisation — the organic matrix (osteoid) is laid down but not adequately mineralised with calcium and phosphate due to Vitamin D deficiency, calcium deficiency, phosphate deficiency, or hypophosphataemia. Bones become soft, painful, deformable, and prone to fracture or deformity.
types.rickets_features: Children: softening and deformity of growing bones. Clinical: bow legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum); bowing of forearms; frontal bossing; delayed dentition; Harrison's groove (horizontal depression at lower chest margin from softened ribs); costochondral junction swelling ('rickety rosary'); craniotabes (soft parietal/occipital bones in infants); widening of metaphyses on X-ray (cupping, fraying); delayed fontanelle closure; reduced height; irritability
types.osteomalacia_features: Adults: bone pain (particularly back, hips, ribs, feet — worst on weight-bearing); proximal muscle weakness (particularly hip girdle — difficulty climbing stairs, rising from chair — 'waddling gait'); Looser zones (pseudofractures — pathognomonic on X-ray — radiolucent bands perpendicular to bone surface); stress fractures; bone tenderness on palpation (tibial tenderness); diffuse aches mistaken for fibromyalgia or arthritis

types_of_rickets.vitamin_D_deficiency_rickets: Most common globally — Vitamin D deficiency causes calcium malabsorption
types_of_rickets.calcium_deficiency_rickets: Endemic in Nigeria, South Africa, and parts of India — adequate Vitamin D but inadequate dietary calcium; responds to calcium supplementation alone
types_of_rickets.vitamin_D_resistant_rickets: Familial hypophosphataemia (XLH — X-linked hypophosphataemia) — PHEX gene mutations causing FGF-23 excess and phosphate wasting; does NOT respond to Vitamin D alone
types_of_rickets.vitamin_D_dependent_rickets: Type I (VDDR-I): CYP27B1 mutations — cannot activate Vitamin D; responds to calcitriol. Type II (VDDR-II): VDR mutations — Vitamin D receptor defect; may require massive calcitriol doses or calcium infusion

types.name: Calcium Deficiency in Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD-MBD)
types.description: Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD) — a complex mineral metabolism disorder that develops as GFR falls. Mechanisms: (1) Reduced 1α-hydroxylase activity in damaged kidneys → reduced calcitriol production → reduced calcium absorption; (2) Phosphate retention (reduced GFR → hyperphosphataemia → directly lowers calcium + stimulates PTH); (3) Secondary hyperparathyroidism (compensatory PTH excess) → bone disease (osteitis fibrosa cystica); (4) FGF-23 elevation → further reduces calcitriol.
types.management: Phosphate binders (sevelamer, calcium carbonate — reduce dietary phosphate absorption); active Vitamin D (calcitriol/alfacalcidol — NOT cholecalciferol which requires renal activation); calcimimetics (cinacalcet — sensitises CaSR to calcium, reducing PTH); dialysate calcium optimisation

types.name: Pseudo-Hypoparathyroidism (PHP)
types.description: A rare group of disorders characterised by target organ resistance to PTH (rather than PTH deficiency). PTH levels are HIGH (compensatory), but the kidneys and bones fail to respond normally. Biochemically identical to hypoparathyroidism (low calcium, high phosphate) but HIGH PTH distinguishes it. PHP Type 1a (Albright's Hereditary Osteodystrophy — AHO): short stature, round face, short 4th metacarpal, subcutaneous calcifications (classic phenotype). Treatment: calcium + calcitriol (same as hypoparathyroidism); PTH replacement does not help (resistance to PTH).
types.diagnosis: Low calcium + high phosphate + HIGH PTH + normal renal function = PTH resistance (PHP) vs hypoparathyroidism (low/normal PTH)

severity_levels.name: Mild Calcium Deficiency / Mild Hypocalcaemia
severity_levels.description: Subclinical or minimally symptomatic; often discovered on routine blood tests or DEXA scanning
severity_levels.serum_calcium: 8.0-8.4 mg/dL corrected total calcium (borderline low); or Ionised calcium 1.10-1.17 mmol/L
severity_levels.symptoms: Usually asymptomatic; possible mild tingling, muscle cramps (especially nocturnal leg cramps), mild fatigue
severity_levels.urgency: Non-urgent; manage with dietary calcium, Vitamin D supplementation, lifestyle measures
severity_levels.management: Dietary calcium optimisation; Vitamin D supplementation (if deficient); lifestyle modification (weight-bearing exercise); reassess blood tests and DEXA in 1-2 years

severity_levels.name: Moderate Calcium Deficiency / Moderate Hypocalcaemia
severity_levels.description: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia or significant bone loss requiring active treatment
severity_levels.serum_calcium: 7.5-7.9 mg/dL corrected total calcium; Ionised calcium 0.90-1.10 mmol/L
severity_levels.symptoms: Perioral numbness; finger and toe tingling (paraesthesiae); muscle cramps and spasms; positive Chvostek's sign; mild cognitive effects; bone pain (osteomalacia)
severity_levels.management: Oral calcium supplements; Vitamin D3 supplementation (if deficient); treat underlying cause; antiresorptive therapy for osteoporosis (bisphosphonates); specialist endocrinology/rheumatology referral

severity_levels.name: Severe Hypocalcaemia
severity_levels.description: Clinically significant neuromuscular and cardiac manifestations
severity_levels.serum_calcium: 7.0-7.4 mg/dL corrected total calcium; Ionised calcium 0.80-0.90 mmol/L
severity_levels.symptoms: Tetany (carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm); positive Trousseau's sign; seizures; cardiac conduction abnormalities (prolonged QT interval on ECG); severe muscle cramps; confusion; arrhythmias
severity_levels.urgency: URGENT — hospital admission for monitoring and IV calcium
severity_levels.management: IV calcium gluconate infusion; cardiac monitoring (ECG); treat underlying cause; transition to oral calcium + calcitriol for long-term management

severity_levels.name: Critical / Life-Threatening Hypocalcaemia
severity_levels.description: Imminent cardiac or respiratory arrest from hypocalcaemia-related complications
severity_levels.serum_calcium: <7.0 mg/dL corrected total calcium; Ionised calcium <0.80 mmol/L
severity_levels.symptoms: Severe tetany; laryngospasm causing respiratory distress; intractable seizures; cardiac arrhythmias (torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation); severe hypotension; loss of consciousness
severity_levels.urgency: EMERGENCY — ICU-level care; immediate IV calcium; resuscitation team on standby
severity_levels.management: EMERGENCY: IV calcium gluconate 10% (1-2 ampoules = 90-180mg elemental calcium) IV STAT over 10 minutes; then continuous calcium infusion; continuous cardiac monitoring; ICU admission; anaesthesia for laryngospasm; benzodiazepines for seizures; simultaneous correction of magnesium, phosphate, potassium

three_mechanisms: Inadequate intake — insufficient dietary calcium to meet daily requirements
Impaired absorption — Vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption syndromes, medications
Increased loss or utilisation — blood loss, increased bone turnover, renal loss

primary_causes.detail: THE MOST COMMON CAUSE of calcium malabsorption globally. Vitamin D is essential for intestinal calcium absorption — without adequate calcitriol, only 5-10% of dietary calcium is absorbed (vs 30-40% with adequate Vitamin D). Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets (children) and osteomalacia (adults) even with adequate dietary calcium intake. In India: 40-70% of the population is Vitamin D deficient despite abundant sunlight — due to: melanin (reduces UV-B skin penetration), indoor lifestyle, air pollution (blocks UV-B), modest skin coverage, fear of skin darkening.
primary_causes.prevalence_india: 40-70% of Indian population has Vitamin D insufficiency (<30 ng/mL 25-OH-Vitamin D); 20-30% have severe deficiency (<12 ng/mL)

primary_causes.detail: Insufficient calcium in daily diet below requirements. Particularly common in: vegans (no dairy or milk); lactose-intolerant individuals avoiding all dairy; populations with low dairy intake; elderly with poor appetite and dietary restriction; children and adolescents who consume few dairy products. India: average Indian diet provides 300-400mg calcium/day from predominantly vegetarian sources — significantly below the 600-1000mg recommended.
primary_causes.most_affected: Vegans; lactose-intolerant; elderly; adolescents; pregnant/lactating women; post-gastrectomy patients

primary_causes.detail: The most common cause of acute and chronic hypocalcaemia in adults. PTH is essential for maintaining calcium homeostasis — its loss causes calcium to fall precipitously. Post-thyroidectomy (total) and parathyroid surgery carry significant hypoparathyroidism risk from inadvertent removal or devascularisation of all four parathyroid glands. Temporary transient hypoparathyroidism is very common post-thyroidectomy (24-72 hours); permanent hypoparathyroidism occurs in 1-5% of total thyroidectomies.
primary_causes.other_surgical_causes: Parathyroidectomy; radical neck dissection; head and neck cancer surgery

primary_causes.detail: A critically important and commonly missed cause of hypocalcaemia. Magnesium is REQUIRED for PTH secretion — hypomagnesaemia suppresses PTH release AND causes peripheral resistance to PTH action. Hypocalcaemia in the setting of hypomagnesaemia will NOT correct with calcium replacement alone — MUST CORRECT MAGNESIUM FIRST. This is one of the most common pitfalls in hypocalcaemia management.
primary_causes.causes_of_hypomagnesaemia: Alcohol misuse; malabsorption; prolonged PPI use; loop diuretics; cisplatin chemotherapy; refeeding syndrome; severe diarrhoea

primary_causes.detail: Failing kidneys reduce 1α-hydroxylase activity — the enzyme that converts 25(OH)D to active calcitriol. Result: calcitriol deficiency → reduced intestinal calcium absorption → hypocalcaemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism. Phosphate retention in CKD also directly lowers calcium. Progressive CKD develops CKD-MBD (Mineral Bone Disorder) — a complex spectrum of calcium, phosphate, PTH, calcitriol, and FGF-23 dysregulation causing renal osteodystrophy.
primary_causes.prevalence: CKD affects ~10% of adults globally; virtually all patients with eGFR <30 mL/min develop some degree of CKD-MBD

primary_causes.detail: Conditions causing impaired absorption of calcium and fat-soluble Vitamin D from the small intestine: Coeliac disease (villous atrophy — duodenal/proximal jejunal absorption impaired); Crohn's disease involving small intestine; Bariatric surgery (gastric bypass diverts food from duodenum — primary calcium absorption site; sleeve gastrectomy reduces acid needed to solubilise calcium); Short bowel syndrome; Chronic pancreatic insufficiency (fat malabsorption → Vitamin D malabsorption); Primary biliary cholangitis.
primary_causes.clinical_note: Hypocalcaemia resistant to oral calcium supplementation should always prompt investigation of malabsorption

primary_causes.detail: Long-term corticosteroid therapy (prednisolone ≥7.5mg/day for >3 months) is the most common cause of SECONDARY OSTEOPOROSIS. Mechanisms: (1) Directly reduce intestinal calcium absorption by suppressing Vitamin D-dependent calcium transport; (2) Increase renal calcium excretion; (3) Suppress osteoblast function (bone formation); (4) Promote osteoclast activity (bone resorption); (5) Suppress gonadotropins → hypogonadism → accelerated bone loss. Fracture risk increases within 3-6 months of starting corticosteroids.
primary_causes.drugs_causing: Prednisolone, dexamethasone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone — all at significant doses; inhaled corticosteroids at high doses (beclomethasone >1500mcg/day equivalent)

primary_causes.cause: Medications Reducing Calcium Levels or Bone Density
medications: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) — reduce gastric acid needed to solubilise calcium carbonate; long-term use associated with osteoporosis and hip fractures; switch to calcium citrate (absorbed independently of acid)
Anticonvulsants (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone) — induce CYP450 enzymes → accelerate Vitamin D catabolism → Vitamin D deficiency → calcium malabsorption
Loop diuretics (furosemide) — increase renal calcium excretion (hypercalciuria)
Bisphosphonates in excess — correct cause of hypocalcaemia; paradoxically can worsen hypocalcaemia if given without adequate calcium/Vitamin D pre-loading
Denosumab — RANK-L inhibitor; suppresses bone resorption dramatically; can cause significant hypocalcaemia, particularly in Vitamin D-deficient or CKD patients
Calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) — used in transplant; increase bone loss
Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole — breast cancer treatment) — reduce oestrogen → accelerated bone loss in postmenopausal women
Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT — for prostate cancer) — testosterone deficiency → osteoporosis in men

primary_causes.detail: Oestrogen plays a critical protective role in bone health. It: (1) Suppresses osteoclast activity (via inhibiting RANK-L, promoting OPG); (2) Promotes intestinal calcium absorption; (3) Reduces renal calcium excretion. Menopause causes a dramatic 'bone remodelling uncoupling' — osteoclast activity exceeds osteoblast activity for 5-10 years post-menopause. Bone loss rate: 1-3% per year in early postmenopause (accelerated phase) vs 0.5-1%/year normal ageing. Most vertebral bone loss occurs in the first 10 years post-menopause.
primary_causes.magnitude: Average woman loses 15% of trabecular bone and 10% of cortical bone in the first 10 years post-menopause

primary_causes.detail: A dramatic hypocalcaemia occurring after parathyroidectomy (for hyperparathyroidism) or after correcting hyperthyroidism. Pre-operatively, excess PTH has been causing bone resorption and high turnover. After PTH is removed, the skeleton rapidly recaptures calcium (hungry for mineralisation) — serum calcium falls precipitously within hours. May require IV calcium infusion for days to weeks post-operatively.
primary_causes.management: Aggressive oral and IV calcium loading post-parathyroidectomy; pre-operative Vitamin D optimisation reduces severity

risk_factors: Female sex (lower peak bone mass; post-menopausal oestrogen deficiency)
Increasing age (>50 years)
Family history of osteoporosis or hip fracture in first-degree relative
White or Asian ethnicity (lower peak bone mass than Black populations)
Low body weight (BMI <19) — thin women have low oestrogen and less mechanical bone loading
Sedentary lifestyle / immobility — mechanical loading stimulates bone formation
Smoking — directly toxic to osteoblasts; increases oestrogen catabolism
Alcohol excess (>3 units/day) — directly suppresses osteoblasts; increases fall risk
Calcium-poor diet (vegan, dairy-free, low food variety)
Low sun exposure / Vitamin D deficiency — indoor lifestyle, hijab, north latitude, dark skin
Glucocorticoid use (>3 months)
Thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism; excess thyroxine therapy)
Hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure; amenorrhoea; male hypogonadism)
Prior fragility fracture (after 40 years)
Falls (elderly; reduced muscle strength; impaired balance; postural hypotension; psychoactive medications)
Malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, bariatric surgery)
CKD (eGFR <45 mL/min)
Liver disease (reduced 25-hydroxylation of Vitamin D)
Eating disorders (anorexia nervosa — low calcium intake + amenorrhoea + low body weight → severe osteoporosis in young women)
Elite athlete amenorrhoea (female athletic triad)
Lactase deficiency / lactose intolerance leading to dairy avoidance
Proton pump inhibitor long-term use

symptoms.note: Symptoms depend critically on the SPEED of calcium fall (acute vs chronic) and the SEVERITY of hypocalcaemia. Chronic mild hypocalcaemia may be remarkably well-tolerated and asymptomatic. Acute hypocalcaemia (especially post-surgical) produces dramatic neuromuscular symptoms even at mild-moderate levels. Osteoporosis causes NO symptoms until a fracture occurs — the 'silent thief'.

primary_symptoms.name: Perioral Numbness and Tingling (Perioral Paraesthesiae)
primary_symptoms.description: Numbness and tingling around the mouth (perioral area) — classically described as a 'circle of numbness around the lips' — is the EARLIEST and MOST CHARACTERISTIC symptom of hypocalcaemia. Results from lowered threshold for spontaneous nerve depolarisation when calcium (which stabilises sodium channels) is reduced. Occurs before other symptoms and should always prompt immediate calcium measurement in at-risk patients (post-thyroidectomy, nutritional risk).
primary_symptoms.onset: Often first symptom — occurs at borderline hypocalcaemia (8.0-8.5 mg/dL)
primary_symptoms.significance: Highly specific early warning sign — prompt calcium measurement warranted

primary_symptoms.name: Finger and Toe Tingling (Extremity Paraesthesiae)
primary_symptoms.description: Bilateral tingling, numbness, and pins-and-needles in fingertips and toes — from peripheral nerve hyperexcitability. Usually begins in fingers (especially tips) and toes symmetrically. If unilateral or dermatomal — suggests nerve compression rather than hypocalcaemia. Worsens with hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis reduces ionised calcium further).

primary_symptoms.name: Muscle Cramps and Spasms
primary_symptoms.description: Painful involuntary muscle contractions — most commonly in the calves (nocturnal leg cramps), forearms, hands, and feet. Calcium is required for muscle relaxation (calcium binds troponin to initiate contraction; calcium pump returns calcium to SR for relaxation — but at low extracellular calcium, muscle membranes are hyperexcitable → prolonged contraction). Hypocalcaemic muscle cramps are characteristically triggered by activity, hyperventilation, or pressure.
primary_symptoms.common_locations: Calf muscles (nocturnal); hands and forearms; feet; facial muscles

primary_symptoms.name: Tetany
primary_symptoms.description: The hallmark of severe hypocalcaemia — sustained, painful, involuntary muscle spasms from uncontrolled peripheral nerve depolarisation. In the HANDS: classical carpopedal spasm — the hand adopts the 'obstetrician's hand' posture: thumb adducted, metacarpophalangeal joints flexed, interphalangeal joints extended, wrist flexed (also called 'main d'accoucheur'). In the FACE: Chvostek's sign (see clinical signs). In the LARYNX: laryngospasm — the most dangerous tetany manifestation, causing stridor and potentially respiratory arrest. Generalised tetany: extreme pain and fear.
primary_symptoms.laryngospasm_warning: Laryngospasm is LIFE-THREATENING — harsh inspiratory stridor with respiratory distress in a hypocalcaemic patient = EMERGENCY; IV calcium gluconate STAT

primary_symptoms.name: Chvostek's Sign (Clinical Sign)
primary_symptoms.description: Tapping the facial nerve (anterior to the ear, over the parotid gland) produces ipsilateral facial muscle twitching — from facial nerve hyperexcitability in hypocalcaemia. Positive in 10-25% of normal individuals (low specificity) but highly sensitive for significant hypocalcaemia when combined with other features. Graded: Grade I — twitch at corner of mouth only; Grade II — twitching of corner of mouth + nose + eye; Grade III — full hemi-facial contraction.
primary_symptoms.clinical_use: Bedside screening for hypocalcaemia; particularly useful post-thyroidectomy/parathyroidectomy monitoring

primary_symptoms.name: Trousseau's Sign (Clinical Sign)
primary_symptoms.description: Inflation of a blood pressure cuff on the upper arm to 20mmHg above systolic for 3 minutes produces CARPOPEDAL SPASM (obstetrician's hand posture — wrist and MCP flexion, IP extension, thumb adduction) in hypocalcaemia. Trousseau's sign is MORE SPECIFIC and SENSITIVE than Chvostek's sign. The cuff occludes arterial flow → localised hypoxia → lowers threshold for nerve depolarisation further. Trousseau's sign positive = significant hypocalcaemia even when total calcium is only borderline.
primary_symptoms.clinical_use: More reliable than Chvostek's sign; perform when hypocalcaemia suspected but calcium borderline low

primary_symptoms.name: Bone Pain, Fragility Fractures, and Bone Deformity
primary_symptoms.description: The skeletal manifestations of calcium deficiency: Osteomalacia — diffuse dull bone pain (particularly weight-bearing areas: back, hips, shins, feet; worst on activity); point tenderness on palpation of bony prominences; proximal muscle weakness. Osteoporosis — typically NO pain until a FRACTURE occurs; fractures from minimal trauma (fragility fractures): vertebral crush fractures (sudden back pain; progressive kyphosis — 'Dowager's hump'); hip fracture (fall from standing height); Colles' fracture (wrist fracture on outstretched hand). Rickets — bow legs or knock knees; stunted growth; bossing of skull; rickety rosary (chest).
primary_symptoms.osteoporosis_note: Vertebral fractures are often SILENT — gradual loss of height (>2cm height loss is a clinical indicator to investigate for vertebral fractures)

secondary_symptoms: Neuropsychiatric symptoms — anxiety, depression, irritability, cognitive impairment, memory problems, psychosis (rare — from chronic hypocalcaemia affecting dopaminergic pathways; basal ganglia calcification visible on CT in long-standing hypoparathyroidism)
Seizures — from profound hypocalcaemia causing cortical hyperexcitability; all types (tonic-clonic, focal, absence); first presentation may be seizure without preceding tetany

Prolonged QT interval on ECG — calcium stabilises cardiac sodium channels; hypocalcaemia prolongs action potential repolarisation → QT prolongation → risk of torsades de pointes → ventricular fibrillation; monitor ECG in moderate-severe hypocalcaemia

Dental and oral abnormalities — in chronic childhood calcium/Vitamin D deficiency: enamel hypoplasia (pitting, horizontal ridges on enamel), delayed dentition, increased dental caries, dental abscess formation; adult tooth loss
Dry skin, eczema, coarse hair — from calcium's role in epidermal cell differentiation and keratinisation; poor skin turgor
Brittle nails with ridging — from impaired nail keratinisation
Hair loss (alopecia) — chronic hypoparathyroidism causes diffuse scalp hair thinning; alopecia areata associated with autoimmune hypoparathyroidism (APS-1)

Cataracts — subcapsular cataracts develop in 30-50% of patients with chronic hypoparathyroidism; from calcium-dependent lens epithelial cell dehydration and protein precipitation; bilateral; develop years after disease onset
Basal ganglia calcification — symmetrical intracranial calcification visible on CT in chronic hypoparathyroidism (Fahr's syndrome pattern); may cause parkinsonism, chorea, dystonia
Papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure — from cerebral oedema in severe acute hypocalcaemia (rare)

Cardiac failure and cardiomyopathy — chronic profound hypocalcaemia can cause reversible dilated cardiomyopathy (calcium is essential for cardiac muscle contraction); rare but important; normalises with calcium repletion

Height loss and kyphosis ('Dowager's hump') — from multiple vertebral crush fractures in osteoporosis; progressive kyphosis from posterior wedging of thoracic vertebrae; each vertebral fracture causes ~1-2cm height reduction

rickets: Craniotabes — softening of parietal and occipital bones (early sign in infants); skull feels like a ping-pong ball on gentle pressure
Frontal bossing — prominence of frontal bones
Rickety rosary — beading at costochondral junctions (enlarged costochondral junction knobs)
Harrison's groove — horizontal indentation at lower chest margin where diaphragm inserts into softened ribs
Delayed eruption of teeth with enamel hypoplasia
Bow legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum) — the most visible deformity
Wrist and ankle widening on examination (metaphyseal widening)
Hypotonia (poor muscle tone); delayed motor milestones

diagnostic_approach.overview: Diagnosis proceeds through three levels: (1) Confirm calcium deficiency/hypocalcaemia — serum calcium with albumin correction and ionised calcium; (2) Identify the cause — PTH, Vitamin D, phosphate, magnesium, renal function; (3) Assess skeletal consequences — DEXA scan (bone mineral density), X-ray (rickets/osteomalacia).
diagnostic_approach.always_correct_for_albumin: Total calcium is unreliable without albumin correction — low albumin (common in sick patients) gives a falsely low total calcium. ALWAYS correct calcium: Corrected calcium = Total calcium + 0.8 × (4.0 − Albumin). Better still, measure IONISED calcium directly.

medical_history: Calcium intake history: dairy products (how often); non-dairy calcium sources; dietary restrictions (vegan, lactose intolerance, dairy allergy); total estimated daily calcium intake
Vitamin D exposure: sun exposure frequency and duration; use of sunscreen; skin tone; indoor vs outdoor lifestyle; latitude and seasonal variation
Medication history: PPIs, corticosteroids, loop diuretics, anticonvulsants, bisphosphonates, denosumab, aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy, calcineurin inhibitors, cisplatin, lithium
Surgical history: thyroidectomy (total or near-total); parathyroidectomy; neck dissection; bariatric surgery (gastric bypass — reduces calcium absorption); intestinal resection
Symptoms: perioral numbness; finger/toe tingling; muscle cramps; tetany; seizures; bone pain; fractures from minimal trauma; height loss; back pain
Menstrual history in women: age at menopause; regularity of periods; premature ovarian insufficiency (POI); hormonal contraception or HRT use
Falls history in elderly: number of falls; circumstances; dizziness (postural hypotension); medications causing dizziness (antihypertensives, diuretics, antidepressants)
GI symptoms: diarrhoea (malabsorption — coeliac, Crohn's, pancreatic insufficiency); bloating; fatty stools (steatorrhoea — fat-soluble Vitamin D malabsorption)
Alcohol use (suppresses osteoblasts; associated with nutritional deficiencies)
Family history: osteoporosis; hip fracture in parent or sibling; early menopause; coeliac disease
physical_examination: Chvostek's sign: tap facial nerve anterior to tragus of ear; observe for facial twitch ipsilaterally
Trousseau's sign: inflate BP cuff 20 mmHg above systolic for 3 minutes; positive = carpopedal spasm
Assessment of tetany: observe hand and foot posture; test for laryngospasm (stridor)

Bone examination: spinal percussion (vertebral tenderness); tibial tenderness (shin bone tenderness = osteomalacia); rib cage palpation (rickety rosary, Harrison's groove); limb alignment (bow legs or knock knees in children)
Height measurement: current height vs historical maximum (>2cm reduction suggests vertebral fractures); standing versus sitting height
Postural kyphosis: Dowager's hump in osteoporotic women; measure occiput-to-wall distance (normally 0; increased in kyphosis)
Muscle strength: proximal muscle weakness (difficulty rising from chair without armrests; hip extension strength — waddling gait in osteomalacia)
Eye examination: posterior subcapsular lens opacity (cataracts — in chronic hypoparathyroidism)
Skin, hair, nails: dry skin; coarse hair; ridged or brittle nails; alopecia
Cardiac: heart rate and rhythm (arrhythmia from hypocalcaemia); blood pressure
Neurological: cognitive assessment; signs of basal ganglia involvement (tremor, rigidity, chorea) in chronic hypoparathyroidism

diagnostic_tests.description: The primary test for assessing calcium status. ALWAYS measure serum albumin simultaneously — low albumin gives falsely low total calcium. Apply correction formula: Corrected Ca (mg/dL) = Total Ca (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4.0 − Albumin g/dL). Normal total calcium: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL. Both hypocalcaemia (<8.5 mg/dL) and hypercalcaemia (>10.5 mg/dL) require investigation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for and confirm hypocalcaemia; basis for further investigations
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Corrected calcium <8.5 mg/dL: hypocalcaemia; 8.0-8.4: mild; 7.5-7.9: moderate; <7.5: severe; <7.0: critical emergency
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Total calcium unreliable without albumin correction — always apply formula or measure ionised calcium

diagnostic_tests.type: Blood — Biochemical — Gold Standard for Hypocalcaemia
diagnostic_tests.description: Direct measurement of the physiologically active FREE calcium fraction — not affected by albumin levels, acid-base status, or binding proteins. The most accurate test for true calcium status. Normal ionised calcium: 1.12-1.30 mmol/L (4.5-5.2 mg/dL). Requires special collection (heparinised tube; kept on ice; processed rapidly) or point-of-care blood gas analyser (most ICUs and emergency departments measure it on the blood gas machine).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Definitive measure of calcium status; most reliable in critically ill patients (low albumin, acid-base disorders); monitoring in ICU and acute hypocalcaemia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ionised Ca <1.12 mmol/L: hypocalcaemia; <1.00: moderate; <0.90: severe; <0.80: critical

diagnostic_tests.type: Blood — Endocrine — CRITICAL for identifying cause
diagnostic_tests.description: PTH is the KEY diagnostic test to identify the CAUSE of hypocalcaemia. PTH interpretation requires simultaneous calcium level: LOW calcium + LOW/normal PTH = hypoparathyroidism or magnesium deficiency. LOW calcium + HIGH PTH = secondary hyperparathyroidism (appropriate response to calcium deficiency — Vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, CKD). LOW calcium + HIGH PTH in the context of PHP = PTH resistance.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify cause of hypocalcaemia; differentiate hypoparathyroidism from secondary hyperparathyroidism; diagnose hyperparathyroidism if calcium is HIGH
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal PTH: 10-65 pg/mL (varies by lab). Low calcium + LOW PTH (<10 pg/mL): hypoparathyroidism. Low calcium + HIGH PTH (>65 pg/mL): secondary hyperparathyroidism (Vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, CKD). Critically important: PTH is measured with calcium — interpret together.

diagnostic_tests.description: The storage form of Vitamin D — the best indicator of Vitamin D status (reflects dietary intake and skin synthesis). NOT the active form (calcitriol/1,25-OH2D) — calcitriol levels fluctuate too much and are unreliable for status assessment. 25-OH Vitamin D is the standard clinical Vitamin D test.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose Vitamin D deficiency as cause of calcium malabsorption; guide supplementation dosing; monitor treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: 25-OH Vitamin D levels: <10 ng/mL (25 nmol/L): severe deficiency; 10-20 ng/mL: deficiency; 20-30 ng/mL: insufficiency; 30-80 ng/mL: sufficient (optimal); >100 ng/mL: possible toxicity risk (>150 ng/mL: toxicity)
diagnostic_tests.india_note: 40-70% of Indians have levels <20 ng/mL despite abundant sunlight — melanin, indoor lifestyle, air pollution, and dietary factors all contribute

diagnostic_tests.description: Phosphate levels help identify the CAUSE of hypocalcaemia. LOW calcium + HIGH phosphate: hypoparathyroidism (no PTH phosphaturia → phosphate retained) or CKD (reduced renal excretion). LOW calcium + LOW/normal phosphate: Vitamin D deficiency (intestinal phosphate absorption also reduced); malabsorption; secondary hyperparathyroidism causes phosphaturia. LOW phosphate + normal or elevated calcium: X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH) or other phosphate-wasting conditions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Narrow differential diagnosis of hypocalcaemia; diagnose phosphate-wasting conditions (rickets subtypes)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hypoparathyroidism: Low Ca + HIGH phosphate; Vitamin D deficiency: Low Ca + LOW-NORMAL phosphate; CKD: Low Ca + HIGH phosphate + low calcitriol

diagnostic_tests.description: MUST ALWAYS CHECK MAGNESIUM in any patient with hypocalcaemia. Hypomagnesaemia (<0.7 mmol/L) suppresses PTH secretion and causes PTH resistance → hypocalcaemia that CANNOT BE CORRECTED without first replacing magnesium. This is one of the most important and commonly overlooked aspects of hypocalcaemia management.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify magnesium deficiency as a reversible cause of hypocalcaemia; guide treatment (must correct Mg before Ca will normalise)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Mg <0.7 mmol/L (<1.8 mg/dL): hypomagnesaemia — treat WITH magnesium FIRST; hypocalcaemia will not correct until Mg is normalised

diagnostic_tests.description: Renal function determines whether hypocalcaemia is from CKD (reduced calcitriol production) — the treatment is calcitriol (active form of Vitamin D) NOT cholecalciferol (requires renal 1α-hydroxylation which is impaired in CKD). CKD also determines safe dosing of calcium and Vitamin D supplements.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose CKD as cause of hypocalcaemia; guide appropriate Vitamin D choice (calcitriol/alfacalcidol for CKD — NOT standard cholecalciferol); dose-adjust supplements
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: eGFR <30 mL/min: CKD Stage 4-5; significant impairment of calcitriol production; use active Vitamin D analogues

diagnostic_tests.test_name: DEXA Scan (Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry) — Bone Mineral Density
diagnostic_tests.type: Imaging — Gold Standard for Osteoporosis Diagnosis
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard investigation for osteoporosis — measures Bone Mineral Density (BMD) at lumbar spine (L1-L4) and femoral neck/total hip. Results expressed as T-score (comparison to young adult peak bone mass — the diagnosis) and Z-score (comparison to age-matched peers — helps identify secondary osteoporosis). FRAX tool (WHO fracture risk assessment) combines BMD with clinical risk factors to calculate 10-year major osteoporotic fracture probability — guides treatment threshold.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose osteoporosis (T-score ≤ −2.5); assess fracture risk (FRAX score); monitor treatment response (repeat DEXA every 1-2 years on treatment)
diagnostic_tests.who_criteria: T-score > -1.0: Normal; -1.0 to -2.5: Osteopenia; ≤ -2.5: Osteoporosis; ≤ -2.5 + fragility fracture: Severe osteoporosis
diagnostic_tests.who_should_have_dexa: All women ≥65 years; postmenopausal women <65 with ≥1 risk factor; men ≥70 years; men 50-70 with risk factors; any person with a fragility fracture after 50; patients on long-term corticosteroids (≥3 months); secondary osteoporosis causes
diagnostic_tests.india_note: DEXA is available in most tertiary centres and many tier-2 cities in India; remains underutilised — recommendation: DEXA for all postmenopausal women >50 years with any risk factor

diagnostic_tests.test_name: FRAX Score (WHO Fracture Risk Assessment Tool)
diagnostic_tests.description: Online calculator (www.sheffield.ac.uk/FRAX) that combines BMD (if available) with clinical risk factors to estimate 10-year probability of major osteoporotic fracture (hip, vertebral, forearm, shoulder) and hip fracture specifically. Can be used WITHOUT BMD for initial risk stratification. Country-specific versions available including for India.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Estimate 10-year fracture risk; guide treatment decisions (treat if 10-year major fracture probability >20%, or hip fracture >3% — USA thresholds; country-specific thresholds apply)
diagnostic_tests.input_variables: Age; sex; BMI; prior fragility fracture; parental hip fracture; current smoking; ≥3 units alcohol/day; glucocorticoid use; rheumatoid arthritis; secondary osteoporosis; BMD (optional)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Spine and Hip X-Rays / Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Lateral thoracic and lumbar spine X-rays identify vertebral fractures — many are clinically silent. VFA (Vertebral Fracture Assessment): low-dose lateral spine imaging performed on DEXA machine during bone density scan — convenient, low radiation, detects vertebral deformity. A vertebral fracture on X-ray is itself an indication for osteoporosis treatment regardless of DEXA T-score.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect vertebral fractures (often silent); diagnose osteomalacia (Looser zones/pseudofractures on weight-bearing bones — pathognomonic); diagnose rickets (cupping and fraying of metaphyses; widened growth plates)
diagnostic_tests.looser_zones: Looser zones (Milkman pseudofractures): PATHOGNOMONIC of osteomalacia; radiolucent bands perpendicular to bone cortex; common at medial femoral neck, pubic rami, scapular margin, ribs

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures daily urinary calcium output. Helps distinguish: hypercalciuria (excessive urinary calcium loss — familial hypercalciuria, loop diuretic use, hyperparathyroidism) vs hypocalciuria (low urinary calcium — from dietary deficiency or malabsorption). Essential monitoring in hypoparathyroidism treatment — calcium + calcitriol treatment must be titrated to avoid hypercalciuria and renal stones.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose familial hypercalciuria; guide calcium supplement dosing in hypoparathyroidism (target <4mg/kg/day to avoid renal stone risk); assess calcium balance
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: 100-300mg/day (women); 100-350mg/day (men); <100mg/day: hypocalciuria (dietary deficiency/malabsorption); >350mg/day: hypercalciuria (idiopathic, hyperparathyroidism, hypervitaminosis D)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Bone Turnover Markers (BTMs) — Serum CTX, P1NP
diagnostic_tests.description: Markers of bone remodelling activity. CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of Type I collagen): marker of bone RESORPTION (released by osteoclasts). P1NP (N-terminal propeptide of procollagen Type I): marker of bone FORMATION (released by osteoblasts). Useful for: monitoring antiresorptive treatment response (CTX falls within 3-6 months of bisphosphonate therapy); identifying high turnover osteoporosis; distinguishing osteoporosis from osteomalacia (very high P1NP and low CTX in osteomalacia — osteoid is formed but not mineralised).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Monitor treatment response; assess bone remodelling activity; distinguish osteoporosis from osteomalacia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CTX >500 pg/mL (premenopausal women) or >400 pg/mL (men): high bone resorption. Successful bisphosphonate treatment: CTX falls >50-60% from baseline within 3 months.

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Coeliac Disease Serology (TTG IgA, Total IgA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Coeliac disease causes malabsorption of calcium, Vitamin D, and other fat-soluble vitamins through villous atrophy. Should be tested in all patients with: unexplained osteoporosis; unexplained hypocalcaemia or Vitamin D deficiency resistant to supplementation; IDA + hypocalcaemia combination.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude coeliac disease as cause of calcium and Vitamin D malabsorption

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in moderate-severe hypocalcaemia. Calcium stabilises cardiac sodium channels — hypocalcaemia causes characteristic QT interval prolongation. QTc (corrected QT) >500ms significantly increases risk of torsades de pointes (a potentially fatal polymorphic ventricular tachycardia). Monitor ECG during IV calcium replacement to confirm improvement.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect QT prolongation (cardiac risk of hypocalcaemia); guide urgency of treatment; monitor response to IV calcium
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: QTc >440ms (men) or >460ms (women): prolonged. QTc >500ms: high risk of arrhythmia — urgent IV calcium. Hypocalcaemia characteristically prolongs ST segment (flat long ST → prolonged QT).

medicines.note: Treatment of calcium deficiency must address both the deficiency itself (calcium and Vitamin D supplementation) and the UNDERLYING CAUSE (malabsorption, hypoparathyroidism, CKD, medication review). Calcium supplementation ALONE is insufficient without concurrent Vitamin D to ensure absorption. For osteoporosis, treatment also requires antiresorptive or anabolic bone agents. All medications must be prescribed by a licensed physician or endocrinologist.
treatment_principles: 1. EMERGENCY hypocalcaemia (tetany, laryngospasm, arrhythmia): IV calcium gluconate STAT
2. Correct Vitamin D deficiency FIRST (or simultaneously with calcium — it is futile to supplement calcium without Vitamin D)
3. ALWAYS check and correct magnesium — hypomagnesaemia prevents calcium normalisation
4. Choose the RIGHT calcium formulation: calcium citrate if on PPIs or achlorhydria (acid-independent absorption); calcium carbonate with meals and adequate acid
5. Dose calcium throughout the day (not one large dose) — absorption is saturable at ~500mg elemental calcium per dose; split doses maximise absorption
6. Osteoporosis: calcium + Vitamin D is the FOUNDATION; add antiresorptive or anabolic therapy based on fracture risk
7. Treat underlying cause: stop offending medications where possible; treat coeliac, hypoparathyroidism, CKD-MBD appropriately

categories.purpose: Rapid correction of severe or symptomatic acute hypocalcaemia — tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, QT prolongation, cardiac arrhythmia.

medicines.name: Calcium Gluconate 10% IV
medicines.dosage: ACUTE TETANY/EMERGENCY: 10-20mL of 10% calcium gluconate (= 90-180mg elemental calcium) IV slowly over 10-20 minutes (NEVER BOLUS — rapid injection causes cardiac arrest); followed by continuous infusion of 0.5-2mg/kg/hour elemental calcium. POST-SURGICAL prophylaxis: 1g calcium gluconate IV over 10 min; then repeat or infuse as guided by serum calcium monitoring
medicines.use_case: EMERGENCY treatment of acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, QTc >500ms); post-parathyroidectomy/thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia; hungry bone syndrome; severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia from any cause
medicines.mechanism: Rapidly raises ionised calcium by providing free calcium ions; calcium gluconate is the PREFERRED IV form (less tissue necrosis than calcium chloride if extravasation occurs)
side_effects: Bradycardia and cardiac arrest if given too rapidly — ALWAYS give slowly
Peripheral vein irritation (extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis — use central line for concentrated or high-dose infusions)
Flushing and warmth
Nausea
medicines.monitoring: Cardiac monitoring throughout IV infusion; ionised calcium every 1-4 hours; Mg and phosphate
medicines.note: Calcium gluconate (9% elemental calcium) contains LESS elemental calcium per mL than calcium chloride (27% elemental) — calcium gluconate preferred peripherally due to lower tissue toxicity on extravasation

medicines.name: Calcium Chloride 10% IV
medicines.dosage: 5-10mL 10% calcium chloride (= 136-272mg elemental calcium) IV slowly; used in CARDIAC RESUSCITATION only
medicines.use_case: Cardiac arrest with hypocalcaemia; calcium channel blocker overdose; massive transfusion protocol (citrate-chelated calcium); hypermagnesaemia; hyperkalaemia (stabilises cardiac membrane)
side_effects: Severe tissue necrosis on extravasation — MUST use central venous access only
Bradycardia if given rapidly
Hypotension
medicines.note: Use ONLY via central line — calcium chloride causes severe tissue necrosis if extravasated; calcium gluconate preferred for peripheral administration

categories.category_name: Oral Calcium Supplements — First-Line for Dietary Deficiency
categories.purpose: Correct dietary calcium inadequacy; provide calcium during Vitamin D deficiency correction; supplement calcium in osteoporosis treatment; long-term calcium replacement in hypoparathyroidism.
categories.dosing_principle: Absorption is SATURABLE at ~500mg elemental calcium per dose — split daily dose (e.g., 500mg with breakfast + 500mg with dinner) is significantly better absorbed than one large daily dose. Do NOT exceed 2500mg elemental calcium/day (increased cardiovascular risk at high supplemental doses; kidney stone risk). Dietary calcium is ALWAYS preferable to supplements — supplements carry mild cardiovascular risk that dietary calcium does not.

medicines.name: Calcium Carbonate
medicines.form: Tablet (500mg, 1000mg; containing 200mg and 400mg elemental calcium respectively), Chewable tablet, Oral suspension
medicines.dosage: 1000-2000mg calcium carbonate per day (= 400-800mg elemental calcium) in divided doses; chew or take with meals (requires gastric acid for dissolution and absorption)
medicines.use_case: First-line oral calcium supplement for dietary deficiency; osteoporosis prevention and treatment (foundation calcium supplementation); hypoparathyroidism (with calcitriol)
medicines.elemental_calcium: 40% elemental calcium — highest % of any oral calcium salt; 500mg carbonate = 200mg elemental calcium
medicines.mechanism: Calcium carbonate requires gastric acid for dissolution and conversion to soluble CaCl2 — take WITH MEALS (maximal acid secretion) for best absorption
side_effects: Constipation (most common — manage with adequate fluids and fibre)
Bloating and flatulence (from CO2 generated by acid-carbonate reaction)
Nausea
Rebound acid secretion (milk-alkali syndrome at very high doses: hypercalcaemia + alkalosis + renal impairment)
contraindications: Achlorhydria (reduced or absent gastric acid — use calcium citrate instead)
medicines.note: AVOID in patients on PPIs or H2 blockers — reduced acid impairs absorption; switch to calcium citrate instead

medicines.name: Calcium Citrate
medicines.form: Tablet (950mg citrate = 200mg elemental calcium), Oral powder
medicines.dosage: 1000-2000mg calcium citrate daily in divided doses (= 200-400mg elemental calcium)
medicines.use_case: Calcium supplementation in patients on PPIs or H2 blockers (acid-independent absorption); post-bariatric surgery (gastric bypass — reduced acid); achlorhydria; elderly with reduced acid secretion
medicines.elemental_calcium: 21% elemental calcium — calcium citrate = 200mg elemental calcium per 950mg salt
medicines.mechanism: Calcium citrate does NOT require gastric acid for absorption — solubilised by organic acid chelation; can be taken WITHOUT food on empty stomach
medicines.advantage: Acid-independent absorption — significantly better absorbed than calcium carbonate in patients on PPIs, H2 blockers, post-gastric bypass, or with achlorhydria. Can be taken BETWEEN MEALS.
side_effects: Fewer GI side effects than calcium carbonate (less constipation)
Mild nausea possible
medicines.note: PREFERRED in elderly (often have reduced acid), PPI users, post-bariatric surgery, and patients with inflammatory bowel conditions

medicines.name: Calcium with Vitamin D3 Combination Tablets
medicines.form: Tablet (calcium 500-1000mg + Vitamin D3 200-1000 IU per tablet)
medicines.dosage: 1-2 tablets daily with meals; provides combined calcium + Vitamin D3 supplementation
medicines.use_case: Convenient combined calcium + Vitamin D supplementation for osteoporosis prevention and treatment; dietary deficiency; most widely prescribed combination in India
medicines.note: Most convenient form — combination ensures Vitamin D is always co-administered with calcium; widely used in Indian gynaecology, orthopaedics, and general practice; adjust dose based on individual Vitamin D status

categories.category_name: Vitamin D Supplements — Essential Cofactor for Calcium Absorption
categories.purpose: Correct Vitamin D deficiency to restore intestinal calcium absorption (Vitamin D deficiency reduces absorption from 30% to 5-10%). Vitamin D is ALWAYS required alongside calcium supplementation — supplementing calcium alone without correcting Vitamin D deficiency is largely ineffective.
categories.important_distinction: Vitamin D supplementation requires matching the preparation to the clinical context: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3) — standard supplement for dietary deficiency; requires liver 25-hydroxylation + kidney 1α-hydroxylation; NOT for CKD (kidneys cannot activate it). Calcitriol / Alfacalcidol — ACTIVE or near-active forms; for hypoparathyroidism, CKD (where renal activation is impaired); more potent; narrow therapeutic window.

medicines.name: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3)
medicines.form: Oral sachet/capsule (60,000 IU — most common in India), Tablet (1000 IU, 2000 IU, 5000 IU), IM injection
medicines.dosage: DEFICIENCY TREATMENT: 60,000 IU weekly × 8-12 weeks (India — oral 60K IU sachets widely used); then 60,000 IU monthly maintenance. MAINTENANCE (insufficiency): 1000-2000 IU daily. SEVERE DEFICIENCY: 60,000 IU twice weekly × 4-6 weeks under supervision.
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for nutritional Vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency; osteoporosis foundation supplementation; rickets and osteomalacia (high-dose initially); prevention in elderly, pregnant women, dark-skinned individuals, indoor workers
medicines.mechanism: Cholecalciferol → 25-hydroxylase (liver) → 25(OH)D3 → 1α-hydroxylase (kidney) → 1,25(OH)2D3 (calcitriol — active form); calcitriol binds VDR → increases intestinal calcium absorption, renal calcium reabsorption
side_effects: Vitamin D TOXICITY (hypervitaminosis D) at very high doses — hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria, renal stones, renal failure, metastatic calcification; occurs at sustained supplemental doses >4000 IU/day long-term or very high doses without monitoring; target level 30-80 ng/mL
Nausea, vomiting at toxic doses
Constipation at toxic doses
medicines.monitoring: Check 25-OH Vitamin D levels: at 3 months of treatment (to confirm correction); then 6-monthly maintenance; target 30-60 ng/mL
medicines.india_note: 60,000 IU oral cholecalciferol sachets (e.g., Uprise D3, D-Rise) are the most commonly prescribed Vitamin D formulation in India — practical weekly dosing with high compliance

medicines.name: Ergocalciferol (Vitamin D2)
medicines.dosage: 50,000 IU weekly × 8-12 weeks for deficiency
medicines.use_case: Alternative to D3 where D3 unavailable; vegan-preferred form (D3 is animal-derived — lanolin from sheep wool; D2 is plant/fungal-derived); slightly less potent than D3
medicines.note: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is more effective than D2 (ergocalciferol) at raising serum 25-OH Vitamin D levels — D3 preferred clinically

medicines.name: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 — Active Form)
medicines.dosage: Hypoparathyroidism: 0.25-2 mcg twice daily (titrate to target calcium); CKD: 0.25-1 mcg daily; Post-parathyroidectomy: 0.5-2 mcg daily acutely; adjust based on serum calcium and urine calcium
medicines.use_case: Hypoparathyroidism (FIRST-LINE — bypasses the need for PTH-dependent 1α-hydroxylation); CKD stages 3-5 (kidneys cannot activate cholecalciferol); post-parathyroidectomy; pseudo-hypoparathyroidism; Vitamin D-dependent rickets type I
medicines.mechanism: Calcitriol is the ACTIVE FORM of Vitamin D — directly binds Vitamin D receptor (VDR) without requiring renal or hepatic activation; potently increases intestinal calcium absorption
side_effects: HYPERCALCAEMIA — the primary safety concern with calcitriol (10x more potent than cholecalciferol; narrow therapeutic window)
Hypercalciuria → renal calculi (monitor 24h urine calcium)
Soft tissue calcification (eyes, blood vessels, kidneys) with excessive doses
medicines.monitoring: Serum calcium every 2-4 weeks during dose titration; 24h urinary calcium every 3-6 months; renal function; regular ophthalmology (cataracts in hypoparathyroidism)

medicines.name: Alfacalcidol (1α-hydroxyvitamin D3)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 0.25-2 mcg once daily; CKD and hypoparathyroidism: start 0.25 mcg daily; titrate to serum calcium
medicines.use_case: CKD stages 3-5 (widely used in Indian renal practice); hypoparathyroidism; osteomalacia with liver disease (requires only hepatic activation not renal); osteoporosis in elderly (better tolerated than calcitriol in some populations)
medicines.mechanism: Alfacalcidol (1α-OH-D3) undergoes only HEPATIC 25-hydroxylation (not renal 1α-hydroxylation required) → active 1,25(OH)2D3; thus useful in CKD (bypasses impaired renal 1α-hydroxylase)
medicines.side_effects: Similar to calcitriol; hypercalcaemia risk; monitor serum calcium closely

medicines.name: Magnesium Sulfate (IV) / Magnesium Oxide or Glycinate (Oral)
medicines.dosage: Severe hypomagnesaemia: 2-4g magnesium sulfate IV over 15-30 minutes; then 1-2g/hour IV infusion until normalised. Oral maintenance: 240-480mg elemental magnesium daily (magnesium glycinate or citrate — best tolerated)
medicines.use_case: MANDATORY in hypocalcaemia associated with hypomagnesaemia — correct MAGNESIUM before or simultaneously with calcium; hypocalcaemia will NOT normalise until magnesium is restored
side_effects: IV: flushing; hypotension; loss of deep tendon reflexes (toxicity — stop infusion)
Oral: diarrhoea (common — use magnesium glycinate which is best tolerated)

categories.purpose: Bisphosphonates are first-line pharmacological treatment for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high fracture risk. They inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, reducing bone turnover and significantly increasing bone mineral density. Reduce vertebral fracture risk by 40-70% and hip fracture risk by 30-50%.
categories.note: MUST ensure adequate Vitamin D (>30 ng/mL) and calcium supplementation BEFORE starting bisphosphonates — prescribing bisphosphonates without correcting Vitamin D deficiency risks severe hypocalcaemia ('bisphosphonate-induced hypocalcaemia'). ALWAYS co-prescribe calcium 1000-1200mg/day + Vitamin D3 1000 IU/day with bisphosphonate therapy.

medicines.name: Alendronate (Alendronic Acid)
medicines.dosage: 70mg orally once weekly (most common regimen); or 10mg daily (less convenient; same efficacy); taken FIRST THING IN THE MORNING at least 30-60 minutes before food or any other medication; with full glass of water (200-250mL); remain UPRIGHT for 30-60 minutes after taking (prevents oesophageal irritation)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis; glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; male osteoporosis; Paget's disease of bone
medicines.mechanism: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate — inhibits farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FPP synthase) in the mevalonate pathway within osteoclasts → osteoclast apoptosis → reduced bone resorption
side_effects: Oesophageal irritation/ulceration (MOST IMPORTANT — must take as directed; sit/stand upright 30-60 min; avoid if oesophageal disease; can cause pill-induced oesophagitis)
Musculoskeletal pain (myalgia, arthralgia, bone pain — 'flu-like' symptoms first few weeks)
Osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ) — very rare with oral alendronate; primarily with IV zoledronate/denosumab in cancer; dental hygiene essential

Atypical femoral fractures (AFFs) — very rare; with very long-term use (>5-10 years); prodromal thigh pain — STOP bisphosphonate immediately if AFF suspected; consider bisphosphonate holiday after 5 years
Hypocalcaemia (if Vitamin D deficient — always correct first)
contraindications: Inability to sit/stand upright for 30-60 min
medicines.bisphosphonate_holiday: After 3-5 years oral bisphosphonate: reassess FRAX/BMD; if stable low-moderate risk — consider drug holiday of 1-3 years (bone benefit persists after discontinuation); continue if high risk

medicines.name: Risedronate
medicines.dosage: 35mg once weekly OR 150mg once monthly; same administration requirements as alendronate (morning; upright; water)
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis; glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; similar efficacy to alendronate; possibly slightly better GI tolerability
medicines.side_effects: Similar to alendronate; possibly fewer GI side effects

medicines.name: Zoledronic Acid (Zoledronate)
medicines.dosage: 5mg IV infusion once yearly (osteoporosis); over at least 15 minutes; given by healthcare provider
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (ONCE YEARLY infusion — highest adherence of any bisphosphonate); male osteoporosis; glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; hip fracture prevention (given within 90 days of hip fracture significantly reduces re-fracture and mortality); patients who cannot tolerate or comply with oral bisphosphonates
medicines.advantage: Annual IV infusion — eliminates adherence issues; most convenient; proven hip fracture prevention (HORIZON trials); also treats Paget's disease (single 5mg dose)
side_effects: Acute phase reaction — 'flu-like' illness (fever, myalgia, bone aches) in 30% after first infusion (paracetamol reduces this); usually only after first dose; pre-dose hydration minimises
Osteonecrosis of jaw (rare; dental care before infusion)
Atypical femoral fracture (rare; long-term use)
Renal impairment (check eGFR before each dose — AVOID if eGFR <35; infuse slowly over ≥15 min; ensure good hydration)

medicines.name: Ibandronate
medicines.form: Tablet (150mg monthly oral), IV Infusion (3mg quarterly)
medicines.dosage: 150mg orally once monthly; or 3mg IV every 3 months
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis; particularly suitable for patients who cannot take weekly bisphosphonates; monthly oral or quarterly IV options
medicines.note: Only proven for VERTEBRAL fracture reduction; less evidence for non-vertebral and hip fracture prevention compared to alendronate and zoledronate

medicines.name: Denosumab
medicines.dosage: 60mg SC injection every 6 months (osteoporosis); administered by healthcare provider
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis — particularly when bisphosphonates are contraindicated or poorly tolerated (eGFR <35 — safer in CKD than bisphosphonates); high fracture risk requiring rapid Hb increase; patients who cannot swallow bisphosphonate tablets; cancer patients (prostate cancer on ADT, breast cancer on aromatase inhibitors)
medicines.mechanism: Human monoclonal antibody against RANK-L (Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor κB Ligand) — the key osteoclast differentiation factor; blocks osteoclast formation, function, and survival → profound suppression of bone resorption
side_effects: HYPOCALCAEMIA — can be severe (particularly in Vitamin D deficiency or CKD — ensure Vitamin D >30 ng/mL and calcium supplements started 2 weeks BEFORE denosumab)
Osteonecrosis of jaw (ONJ) — higher risk than oral bisphosphonates; dental examination before starting
Atypical femoral fractures (risk with long-term use)
Infections (cellulitis, urinary tract, respiratory)

Rebound bone loss on DISCONTINUATION — bone turnover rebounds massively after stopping denosumab causing rapid BMD loss and vertebral fracture risk; DO NOT STOP abruptly — transition to bisphosphonate before stopping denosumab
medicines.critical_warning_stopping: NEVER stop denosumab without transitioning to a bisphosphonate — rebound bone resorption after stopping causes multiple vertebral fractures (rebound fracture cascade). Always prescribe alendronate or zoledronate before the last denosumab dose.

categories.purpose: Unlike antiresorptive agents (which reduce bone breakdown), anabolic agents STIMULATE NEW BONE FORMATION — making them particularly valuable in severe osteoporosis, multiple fractures, or when antiresorptive therapy has failed.

medicines.name: Teriparatide (PTH 1-34 Analogue)
medicines.dosage: 20mcg SC daily; maximum 24 months total lifetime use (oncogenicity concern — rat studies showed osteosarcoma at high doses); follow with antiresorptive therapy after course
medicines.use_case: Severe postmenopausal osteoporosis with fractures; glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis; osteoporosis in men; failed antiresorptive therapy; very low BMD (T-score <-3.5); multiple vertebral fractures; high fracture risk requiring rapid BMD improvement
medicines.mechanism: Recombinant PTH(1-34) — intermittent PTH stimulates osteoblast activity > osteoclast activity → net bone formation (paradox: continuous high PTH causes bone loss; pulsatile daily injection stimulates bone formation); increases BMD most rapidly of all osteoporosis treatments (+9% at spine, +3-6% at hip at 18 months)
side_effects: Nausea (mild)
Dizziness
Leg cramps
Transient hypercalcaemia (monitor calcium 1-4 weeks after starting)
Bone pain (initial)
Back pain

Osteosarcoma (only in animal studies at suprapharmacological doses; not shown in humans at therapeutic doses; avoid in: prior radiation, Paget's, bone metastases, hypercalcaemia, open growth plates in children)
medicines.note: Must be followed by antiresorptive therapy (bisphosphonate or denosumab) to consolidate anabolic gains — otherwise BMD is rapidly lost after teriparatide stops

medicines.name: Romosozumab
medicines.dosage: 210mg SC once monthly for 12 months only; follow with antiresorptive therapy
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal women at very high fracture risk; severe osteoporosis not responding to other treatments; after teriparatide course; strongest and most rapid BMD increase of any osteoporosis drug
medicines.mechanism: Anti-sclerostin monoclonal antibody — sclerostin is a Wnt pathway inhibitor produced by osteocytes (suppresses bone formation); romosozumab blocks sclerostin → activates Wnt signalling → osteoblast activity increases AND SIMULTANEOUSLY reduces osteoclast activity (unique dual effect — only osteoporosis drug that simultaneously stimulates formation AND reduces resorption)
side_effects: Hypocalcaemia (correct Vitamin D/calcium before starting)
Arthralgia
CARDIOVASCULAR RISK — FDA black box warning: increased myocardial infarction and stroke risk; contraindicated in patients with prior MI or stroke within 12 months
ONJ; atypical femoral fractures (long-term use)
medicines.black_box_warning: Increased cardiovascular events (MI, stroke) — use with caution in cardiovascular risk patients; contraindicated within 12 months of MI or stroke

categories.category_name: Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) — Oestrogen for Postmenopausal Osteoporosis

medicines.name: Oestrogen ± Progestogen (HRT)
medicines.dosage: Various formulations and doses — individualised; typically: oestradiol 1-2mg orally or 50mcg transdermal patch; add progestogen if uterus intact (prevents endometrial hyperplasia/cancer)
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis prevention — particularly in early postmenopause (<60 years or within 10 years of menopause); also treats menopause symptoms (flushes, sleep); effective at preventing bone loss if started early; Women's Health Initiative (WHI) trial showed significant fracture reduction
medicines.mechanism: Oestrogen inhibits RANK-L-mediated osteoclast recruitment and activity; reduces bone turnover; maintains or increases BMD; also improves calcium absorption and reduces renal calcium loss
side_effects: Breast cancer risk (small increase with combined HRT >5 years; much less with oestrogen-only; transdermal lower risk than oral)
Venous thromboembolism (DVT, PE) — oral HRT; transdermal HRT has minimal VTE risk
Stroke risk (oral HRT; transdermal minimal risk)
Endometrial cancer (with oestrogen alone without progestogen — protect uterus with progestogen)
medicines.prescribing_guidance: Transdermal HRT (patch or gel) preferred over oral (lower VTE and stroke risk); lowest effective dose; re-evaluate annually; generally used for up to 5 years for menopausal symptoms with fracture prevention benefit

medicines.name: Recombinant Human PTH (rhPTH 1-84 — Natpara)
medicines.form: Subcutaneous injection (25-100mcg daily via multi-dose device)
medicines.dosage: 50mcg SC daily; titrate 25-100mcg daily based on serum calcium; used to reduce dependence on high-dose oral calcium and calcitriol
medicines.use_case: Hypoparathyroidism that cannot be adequately controlled with calcium + calcitriol alone; patients with frequent hypocalcaemia or hypercalciuria on conventional therapy; chronic hypoparathyroidism requiring very high oral calcium/calcitriol doses
medicines.mechanism: Replaces missing PTH — promotes renal tubular calcium reabsorption, phosphate excretion, calcitriol synthesis; reduces need for oral calcium/calcitriol supplementation
side_effects: Hypercalcaemia (dose-dependent)
Hypercalciuria (monitor 24h urine Ca)
Nausea, injection site reactions
Osteosarcoma (theoretical — same rat data as teriparatide; rare; avoid in bone metastases, prior radiation, Paget's)
medicines.availability: Available USA, EU; limited availability in India; expensive

categories.category_name: Calcitonin — Adjunct in Osteoporosis and Hypercalcaemia

medicines.name: Salmon Calcitonin (Calcitonin-Salmon)
medicines.form: Nasal spray (200 IU per spray), SC/IM injection (50-200 IU)
medicines.dosage: Osteoporosis: 200 IU nasal spray once daily (alternating nostrils); Paget's disease: 50-100 IU SC/IM daily. Acute hypercalcaemia: 4-8 IU/kg SC/IM every 6-12 hours
medicines.use_case: Postmenopausal osteoporosis — modest BMD benefit; particularly useful for ACUTE VERTEBRAL FRACTURE PAIN (analgesic effect through endorphin release — proven in clinical trials, reduces pain acutely); Paget's disease; acute hypercalcaemia (rapid onset calcium-lowering effect within hours)
medicines.mechanism: Binds calcitonin receptor on osteoclasts — inhibits bone resorption; also acts centrally for analgesia
side_effects: Nasal symptoms (nasal irritation, rhinitis — nasal spray)
Nausea and vomiting (injection)
Flushing
Cancer risk concern — FDA review found marginal increase in cancer with long-term calcitonin (primarily nasal spray); EMA suspended some calcitonin products; use for shortest effective duration
medicines.note: No longer first-line for osteoporosis treatment (bisphosphonates are more effective); useful for acute vertebral fracture pain management and short-term hypercalcaemia

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is the primary foundation of calcium sufficiency. The recommended dietary approach emphasises: maximise calcium-rich food intake; ensure adequate Vitamin D (from sun exposure and/or diet); optimise the calcium-enhancing food environment; and minimise calcium absorption inhibitors. For most people with mild deficiency, dietary optimisation can meet calcium needs without supplements. India-specific context: the predominantly vegetarian Indian diet has many excellent calcium sources — particularly dairy, sesame, ragi/finger millet, drumstick leaves, and amaranth — but cultural practices (excess tea, phytate-rich staple foods, low sun exposure) often undermine calcium nutrition.

recommended_foods.category: Dairy Products — Highest Bioavailability Calcium Sources
recommended_foods.evidence: Very strong — dairy provides highly bioavailable calcium (30-35% absorption rate); lactose in dairy further enhances absorption

items.benefit: 300mg calcium per 250mL glass; highly bioavailable (30-35%); Vitamin D if fortified; protein; B12; potassium; phosphorus. Buffalo milk (widely used in India): 210mg/100mL — slightly higher than cow's milk (120mg/100mL). Warm milk before bed improves sleep and provides calcium for overnight bone maintenance
items.india_context: Doodh (milk) is a culturally significant food in India — widely available; affordable; should be actively promoted for calcium nutrition

items.benefit: 208mg calcium per 100g; high protein (18g/100g); widely used in Indian vegetarian cooking; very versatile in curries, bhurji, sandwiches; one of the best vegetarian calcium sources

items.food: Curd / Dahi (plain yogurt) — whole or low-fat
items.benefit: 120-150mg calcium per 100g; lactose partially hydrolysed (better tolerated in lactose intolerance — many lactose-intolerant people tolerate curd well); probiotics (Lactobacillus) support gut health; Vitamin K2 (menaquinone — directs calcium to bones, away from arteries); versatile in Indian cuisine (raita, kadhi, lassi)
120mg calcium per 250mL; lower fat than full milk; excellent hydration in summer; probiotics; perfect post-meal drink; widely consumed across India

Cheddar: 720mg calcium per 100g; Parmesan: 1184mg per 100g; very concentrated calcium; small portions provide significant calcium; aged hard cheeses also contain Vitamin K2 (menaquinone-9 — bone protective)
items.note: High in saturated fat — limit to small portions; full-fat cheese has more Vitamin K2 than reduced-fat

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — many Indian plant foods provide significant calcium; bioavailability is generally 20-40% (lower than dairy but still meaningful for total intake)

items.food: Ragi / Finger Millet (Nachni) — THE Indian calcium grain
items.benefit: 344mg calcium per 100g (DRY) — extraordinary for a cereal; the HIGHEST calcium content of all major cereals and millets; bioavailability is lower than dairy (~20%) but given the quantity consumed as ragi roti, porridge, ladoo, or mudde (South India) it contributes significantly; also high iron, protein, fibre, B vitamins; gluten-free
items.frequency: Daily as ragi roti, ragi ladoo, ragi mudde, ragi porridge; particularly popular in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra, Tamil Nadu
